relevant_findings.summary: Bare drywall paper facing is highly porous and absorbent. First coat (primer) will be partially absorbed, requiring sufficient mil thickness to seal substrate and provide uniform porosity for subsequent coats.

Joint compound (mud) and paper face have different absorption rates. Without proper priming, 'flashing' occurs where joints show through topcoat due to uneven sheen. PVA or drywall primer equalizes porosity.
New construction drywall accumulates dust from sanding, cutting, and general construction activity. Light dusting or vacuuming of surfaces prior to priming is standard practice.

PVA (polyvinyl acetate) primers are the standard for bare drywall - economical, fast-drying, excellent sealing. High-build primers used for imperfect surfaces. Shellac-based primers only needed for stain-blocking situations (not typical for new construction).
Bare drywall primer coverage typically 300-400 SF/gal due to absorption. More porous than painted surfaces. First coat sees higher material consumption than subsequent coats.

Ceiling work requires different access (scaffolding, lifts) and has ergonomic penalties. Production rates for ceiling priming are typically 15-25% slower than wall priming. Spray application efficiency is more pronounced on ceilings.
Spray is most efficient for large open areas of new construction drywall. Roller is common for smaller areas or when spray is not practical. Brush used only for detail/cut-in work.
New construction typically has defined corners, ceiling lines, and perimeters requiring cut-in or masking. EdgeLF is relevant for brush cut-in at ceiling lines, corners, and around openings.

condition_drivers.description: Industry standard levels 0-5. Level 4 (standard residential) and Level 5 (premium, requires skim coat) affect primer selection and labor. This spec assumes Level 4 as baseline.
condition_drivers.impact: Level 5 finish requires additional inspection and may need high-build primer

condition_drivers.description: Quality of taping and mudding affects priming outcome. Poor joints may need spot-priming or additional coats.
New construction may lack HVAC. Temperature and humidity affect primer dry time and application.
condition_drivers.impact: Production rates may need environmental adjustment

quality_differences.description: Standard prime coat. Single coat PVA primer, standard application, visual inspection for coverage.
Enhanced prime. Same material but with inspection for holidays and touch-up as needed. Light sanding of nibs/debris between prime and topcoat.
Premium prime for Level 5 appearance. May require high-build primer or second prime coat. Thorough inspection and remediation of any imperfections.

failure_modes.cause: Insufficient primer coverage over joint compound, or wrong primer type
failure_modes.prevention: Use proper drywall primer, ensure adequate mil build, inspect before topcoat

failure_modes.cause: Dusty surface not cleaned before priming, or application over damp drywall
failure_modes.prevention: Dust surfaces before priming, verify drywall is dry

failure_modes.cause: Inadequate inspection during application, poor lighting
failure_modes.prevention: Work lighting, systematic coverage pattern, inspection pass

failure_modes.cause: Wrong roller nap, improper technique, or paint viscosity issues
failure_modes.prevention: Use appropriate nap (3/8"-1/2" for smooth drywall), proper loading
failure_modes.severity: Minor to Moderate - affects final appearance

notes_for_materials_manager: PVA primer is the standard product for this spec - economical and effective
High-build primer should be available as option for QT5 or imperfect surfaces
Coverage rates should assume first-coat absorption (300-400 SF/gal)
Roller covers: 3/8" to 1/2" nap for smooth drywall
Spray equipment: airless preferred, 515-517 tip for primers
Include sanding supplies for QT4/QT5 prep between coats
notes_for_sop_librarian: Edge cut-in vs field coverage should be separate tasks
QT4/QT5 add inspection and sanding rounds
Distinguish wall modules from ceiling modules due to different access needs
Spray vs roller should be variant dimension, not different modules
notes_for_estimation_engineer: Ceiling rates should be slower than wall rates (15-25% productivity loss)
Spray is significantly faster than roller for field coverage (2-3x)
Cut-in (edge work) rate is LF-based, not SF-based
QT5 adds approximately 30-50% labor over QT3 baseline
Material consumption higher on bare drywall than repaint work
assumptions: Drywall is Level 4 finish (standard residential) unless specified otherwise
Drywall is dry and properly cured (no moisture issues)
Joint compound work is complete and sanded by drywall contractor
This spec covers PRIMER ONLY - topcoat is separate spec family
Standard ceiling heights (8-10 ft) - high ceilings require height modifiers
Access is available for spray equipment in new construction setting
uncertainties: Exact production rate calibration requires field validation
High-build primer vs standard primer decision criteria need refinement
Environmental condition impact on dry time needs documentation
